summary:
We built UniSim to make 25 years of California wildfire data easier to compare and explore. NASA's MODIS and VIIRS sensors detect fires at different resolutions, meaning the same fire can produce very different hotspot counts. We developed a harmonization method to account for these differences and create a consistent record dating back to 2000.

Users can explore this data through an interactive map, a burning calendar, and layers showing hotspots, smoke, wind, and fire boundaries. We also trained a machine learning model to estimate relative wildfire risk based on historical patterns. Our wildfire simulator uses real terrain, vegetation, and weather data to show how fires might spread under different conditions. Users can change wind settings, add firebreaks, and compare the results with later satellite observations.

We wanted to build something that researchers, emergency planners, and students could actually use, whether they're studying past fires, identifying risk patterns, or experimenting with ways to limit fire spread.
details:
UniSim (by Space Pickles) takes 25 years of California wildfire satellite observations and turns them into an interactive platform for historical analysis, machine learning based risk assessment and fire spread simulation. The central challenge we faced was making the observations from two generations of NASA satellite sensors scientifically comparable.

Data Harmonization

NASA's MODIS (1km) and VIIRS (375m) sensors both detect the same fires, just at different resolutions. If you simply add up the raw hotspot counts from the two sensors you get a very misleading result. We've developed a Python pipeline which filters out the non-vegetation detections and then standardizes detections into fire cell-days at approximately 1km resolution (each active grid cell is counted once per day).

We calibrated a quasi-Poisson regression model using overlapping satellite records from 2012 to 2026 across five latitude bands and seasonal conditions. To deal with the inaccuracies that occurred in the very extreme fire months we adjusted the model and validated it via leave-one-year-out cross-validation, achieving a typical monthly error of 12.2% and a 0.98 correlation on a log scale.

Machine Learning & Risk Outlook

We built a random forest model to estimate relative wildfire risk using a combination of geographic, seasonal and historical burning data across the 707 California grid cells.

A key challenge was preventing data leakage in the historical records (i.e. we were using information which wasn't available at the time of prediction). We dropped all the features which were dependent on hindsight and validated on years we hadn't seen prior to that, getting 0.84 AUC versus a 0.73 baseline.

Precomputed predictions enable the user to explore Low, Medium and High risk levels via an interactive map. These are historical risk outlooks, not operational forecasts.

Wildfire Spread Simulation

Our cellular automaton wildfire simulator models the spread of wildfire between adjacent grid cells based on fuel, terrain and weather. It uses LANDFIRE vegetation data, terrain derived from elevation and historical ERA5 weather.

Users can vary the wind, introduce firebreaks and apply retardant to look at alternative spread scenarios. The system can be used to run simulations based on historical events (e.g. the 2018 Camp Fire) and UniSim can then overlay simulated spread with subsequent satellite observations to compare the two. It's an experimental tool and not for operational prediction.

Platform & Impact

Built on Godot, Python and scikit-learn, UniSim provides an interactive wildfire map, a harmonized burning calendar, configurable environmental layers, risk outlooks and fire simulations. The interface distinguishes between observed, harmonized, simulated and modeled data to communicate their sources and limitations transparently.

Designed for emergency responders, researchers, educators and communities, UniSim makes complex wildfire information more accessible. It's currently focused on California but the framework could be adapted to other areas and with further development could be applied to other natural hazards as well.
